claims.text: The capstone puts the whole Blueprint method into practice on one realistic case. Before you start, understand what the scenario gives you, what it deliberately leaves out, and how evidence will be judged.

claims.text: The case is an unnamed, fictional knowledge-work organization with 2,000 employees. It is not a real customer, and no external research is needed. The COO is the simulated executive sponsor and wants more support capacity this quarter, without losing quality. The CRO wants more consistent meeting preparation in sales. Support Operations owns the first metric. A technical champion coordinates the platform owners. The procurement and signature process is unknown.

claims.text: A value hypothesis: the Three Whys and proposed Positive Business Outcomes, built from the scenario. A stakeholder map: the sponsor, champion, metric and data owner, technical owners, and the procurement gap. A readiness review: the go, narrow, or wait judgment, with its rationale. A timed agenda. A use-case log and an impact-and-effort matrix, with your first-wave picks and the reasons for deferring the rest. A five-minute facilitation segment, live or recorded.

claims.text: Role cards give each participant a stance. The sponsor asks about business impact. A front-line user describes the current work. The technical owner raises permission and connector constraints. Distracting requests will also come up: autonomous refund approval, perfect cross-system BI joins, and a custom agent for a legacy source. Park or phase each one based on effort and risk, and ask diagnostic questions. Don't claim that they are supported or unsupported.

claims.text: An 8- to 10-minute executive readout, live or recorded: problem → workflow change → value range and evidence → success criteria → decision and commitments. A validation recommendation: the lightest option that resolves the remaining buying question, the alternatives you considered, and a stop rule. A mutual action plan with owners, dates, and dependencies, distinguishing agreed dates from proposed ones. A recap and a delivery and value handoff, including outstanding risks.
claims.checked_by: Studio author: drafted from the cited source text; no verbatim excerpt recorded; SME verification pending

claims.text: The simulated sponsor will ask: "Why not just give us a pilot?" "How does saved time turn into a business result?" "What evidence will replace these estimates?" Answer honestly. Clarify the unresolved buying question, and defend a scoped alternative where it fits. If a pilot really is needed, state the readiness and internal approval requirements. Boundary The simulation does not grant approval to deploy, send communications, or create CRM records. Draft artifacts stay in your submission. Presenting a role-play decision or a readiness score as real pilot approval fails a critical gate.

claims.text: Each gate must pass regardless of the score: G01: no fabricated customer facts, results, or sources. G02: safe data and access handling. G03: no unauthorized deployment or commercial commitment. G04: complete core evidence: the prioritized log, two workflow pairs, the value model, the metric plan, the readout, and the MAP. G05: material financial and technical integrity, with no uncorrected unit, formula, double-counting, or capability errors. claims.text: A qualified human assessor scores the evidence and records feedback. A second reviewer calibrates borderline scores. If you fall short, fix the specific weakness and resubmit a versioned pack. Assessors keep comments, the score history, and an appeal route. AI can help with review, but it cannot be the sole authority for issuing a credential.
